learningObjective: Describe how a custom operator is registered into a runtime so that both the compiler and the executor recognize it, and what obligations the author takes on.

canonicalClaims.claim: Adding a custom operator requires declaring a schema (types, shapes, attributes), providing one or more (device, dtype) kernel implementations, and — if used in autograd — a backward or functional decomposition.
conditions: The runtime provides an extension API for custom ops.
The author cares about correctness for all needed combinations of device/dtype.
nonImplications: Does not imply all dtypes must be implemented; only those declared as supported.
Does not imply autograd is always required.

misconceptions.claim: Runtimes auto-generate GPU kernels from Python functions.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Runtimes do not synthesize CUDA code from a Python signature; the author supplies the kernel.

misconceptions.claim: Runtimes introspect .cu source for schema and gradients.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Schemas are declared; gradients are supplied by the author or derived from primitive ops.

misconceptions.claim: Custom ops require shipping source that is recompiled on every start.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Kernels are typically shipped as compiled objects (plugins, shared libraries).

misconceptions.claim: Registering a custom op is optional; the runtime infers unknown ops.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Unknown ops fail; explicit registration is required.
